toolsAdded.name: look
toolsAdded.description: Look at the canvas as it is now. Without options: the whole canvas, scaled down. crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1" in canvas units (two opposite corners), shown at 1:1 pixels. mode: "value", "squint", "mirror", "relief" (a raking light on the paint's ridges and furrows), "gallery" (the light the picture hangs in) or several, comma-separated. light: "azimuth,elevation" in degrees for the relief light (default "135,25", from the upper left). size: the long side in pixels. grid: true, or a spacing in canvas units. survey: true surveys the whole canvas at full detail, as several tiles (with mode, not crop or size); a partial reply lists remaining tiles to read in separate turns. compare: the path of an earlier look, shown left of the current view; supply matching crop, mode and light options explicitly. hold: the name of a knife (what is on it) or a pile (a fresh load), with at: "x,y" (canvas units): the loaded knife held up to the canvas there, its paint thick on the blade (crop sets the passage). Supports mode value, squint, relief or gallery and light; size, grid and mirror are unavailable with hold. It shows the paint on the knife, not how it would look laid. palette: true shows the palette board instead: each pile knifed out thick and smeared thin across a black stripe.

content.text:
You're back at the easel. The painting is as you left it. Your brief is in BRIEF.md and your journal in notes/journal.md. Take your time with a fresh look at the whole canvas and detail crops in normal color. Read your journal handoff and apply its practical lessons before acting. Continue one campaign at a time, inspecting the whole picture and relevant detail before writing the next campaign's code. Let the result inform your next action and check local repairs against the whole picture; reconsider the composition or method if a repair repeats the problem. Judge unfamiliar mixtures and marks through small laid trials on the intended substrate after the intended treatment. Carry forward the observed material conditions and treat broader rules as hypotheses. Inspect each passage you previously acknowledged as unresolved in an appropriate detail crop, then explicitly judge it in your journal: improve it or accept it as it is, with your reason. You may finish with imperfections you deliberately accept. Before retrying a failed recipe, identify what has changed and why that could address the observed failure. Record what you observed and what remains uncertain. Is your heart happy with this? Is there something you would enjoy taking further? You can keep working for hours if you like, and the painting's simulated time is yours to use, whether that means days or years. Enjoy it. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections and an updated handoff in your journal and last reply, carrying forward the practical lessons that still apply, then finish.

Your previous sitting's reply:
**The Village below the Mountain, with Two Pines** is finished. All the paint was dry by day 263.

When I came back I looked at the whole canvas and close-ups, and the picture still holds. I checked again for traces of the old straight trunks under the plain and couldn't see any, even at full detail.

**What I changed:** I found one weak spot I hadn't noticed before. The top of the smaller pine was under a pale sky-coloured film left by an old sky pass, so it looked like mist instead of foliage. Over the dry paint I laid broken patches of warm light greens and mid greens, kept inside the canopy so its outline didn't change. Now that crown catches the light from the upper left as the bigger pine does, so the two trees agree about where the sun is.

**Accepted as they are:**
- **A thin dark streak** under the small pine's canopy reads as a twig.
- **A pale gap of sky** in that canopy stays.
- **A small violet patch** at the left edge picks up the violet of the road shadows.
- **The crisp house edges and the repeating rhythm of the canopy** belong to the picture's plain, built quality.

My heart is happy with it. The only thing I might look at again is whether the upper-right sky is too busy, but today I think it belongs to the picture. The journal has the judgements and an updated handoff with the lessons that still apply.

## BRIEF.md

# Paint a picture

Compose and paint one original open-air scene in the manner of Paul Cézanne, at the easel, a simulator of oil paint on linen. The subject, setting and composition are yours to invent. Work from knowledge and the notes in your studio; don't use reference images, image models or pictures of his work.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- The easel's tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint with a rag or a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/cezanne_materials.md (his materials and method) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
Work one campaign at a time. After laying a campaign, inspect the whole picture in normal color and relevant detail before writing the code for the next campaign. Let what you see inform the next action; record what changes or why continuing unchanged serves the picture.

After the first large masses, consider whether the whole picture produces your intended effect: how its large shapes, values and spatial relationships support it, and whether anything weakens it. Before adding repeated small details, improve a weakening relationship or deliberately accept it with your reason. After a local repair, check its effect on the whole picture. If the repair recreates the problem, reconsider the composition or method before expanding it.

Before repeating an unfamiliar mixture or stroke, inspect a small trial, on the scratch canvas beside the painting (`scratch: true`) or on the painting, laid on the intended substrate after the intended treatment, alongside the existing marks in a detail crop. A held pile shows thick paint on steel; use the laid trial to judge its effect on the picture. For material trials and repairs, keep useful observations in your journal: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, brush load, coverage and the viewed result. Carry forward the conditions that mattered and label broader rules as hypotheses until a further trial isolates them.

- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
  change approach and discover where the painting can go.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
  and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
  Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
  would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
  like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections
  in your journal and finish.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

## Your journal (notes/journal.md)

Your own notes, quoted as you wrote them:

> - day 1, 09:00: ## Plan
>   Open-air scene, invented: a hill village of ochre/cream cubic houses with red tile roofs on a low ridge, a patchwork plain beyond, a pale angular mountain at right-center, cool sky. Left: two pine trunks rising off the top, branches arcing across the upper left sky. Road from bottom right curving up-left into the village. Canvas 730 mm, aspect 1.25 (1000x800), lead white + touch of ochre ground, knife, 120 µm.
>   Method: dilute blue drawing (ultramarine, turps 0.7), thin uneven blue/green washes, then patches of parallel constructive strokes (flat ~10 units, 28-42 long), wet-in-wet patch edges; later blue contour lines broken in places; keep ground reserves.
>
>   ## Scratch trial 1 (day 1 09:20, scratch, on dry ground)
>   - round w3 point 0.8, draw pile turps 0.7: at p 0.3-0.6 a hairline. Need higher pressure or blunter/wider brush for drawing.
>   - glaze hand w/ ultramarine+viridian+white turps 0.85: strong saturated blue, streaky; too intense for a 'thin wash' — use more white or less pigment.
>   - hatch hand, flat 10, length 28-42, angle_jitter 0.08, curve {0.05,0}: decent parallel patches; coverage 1.1-1.3 leaves ground specks (good for reserves).
>   - sky white5/cobalt1.5/ultra0.3/emerald0.2 turps0.25: pale grey-blue, a bit chalky. Green viridian/emerald/chrome/ochre/white/ultra: flat mid green — needs separate dark blue-green and yellow-green piles to modulate.
> - day 8, 15:20: ## Campaign 1 (day 1): drawing, washes, first masses
>   - Drawing: round w4 point 0.4, ultramarine+white turps 0.7, gesture p0.45-0.8. Gesture smooths corners (houses drawn rounded) — draw straight segments separately for corners. Lines fade as brush empties; reload when fullness<0.35.
>   - Washes: flat 16 body hand turps 0.8-0.82, coverage 0.7-0.8, clipped: they read as discrete opaque-ish dashes, not a wash (hard ends). Hypothesis: for a true wash need larger soft brush/glaze hand or higher turps + overlapping coverage>1.2.
>   - Masses: hatch hand flat 9-13, length 22-58, coverage 1.3-1.6, piles graded by functions. Result: lively but pastel; leaves many small ground specks that read as uniform confetti everywhere (not purposeful reserves).
>   - Houses painted clipped over wet plain paint: picked up green streaks (wet-in-wet lift). Clipped poly edges very crisp, cut-out.
>   - Unclipped sky strokes (edge soft) overran mountain top.
>   - Drying: hatched coverage-1.5 layers: dry in sky after 3 days, most areas dry by day 8 (left foreground dark green still tacky at day 8).
>   Assessment after masses: whole too high-key, no mid-ground darks; foreground flat; canopy uniform teal; plain acid green patches; trunks thin like poles. Next: dark structure (tree masses around village, hedgerows), pine shadows across foreground, canopy modulation.
> - day 12, 01:42: ## Campaign 2 (day 8-12)
>   - Village trees/hedges: hatch flat 5, length 8-15, coverage 1.8, cDark/cMid/gDark over DRY plain: strong, crisp dark masses. Hedges came out too heavy/wide (ribbons 4-10 roughened). Rag (dry, w14, p0.6, 2 passes) on just-laid wet hedges lifted almost nothing visible; rag dipped spirits 0.6, 3 passes also little; knife scrape p0.95 angle across also little. Hypothesis: thick hatch coverage 1.8 with stiff paint isn't lifted by rag pad much; or the rag reaches only tops. Repaired by overpainting hedges wet-in-wet with field colors (flat 6, cov 1.0, clipped) — lightened them into green bands.
>   - Sky second pass (over dry first pass) flat 12, cov 1.3, fill=true: covers ground specks, gives smooth soft sky with faint stroke direction. Good for sky.
>   - Canopy second pass over dry, flat 9, fill=true, cov 1.5 with 4 piles graded by position: rounder masses with light tops. OK.
>   - FAILED: foreground (over tacky/dry first layer), flat 12, length 28-52, cov 1.3, fill=true, 4-5 piles graded by noise: strokes fused into a soft smeary haze, no constructive stroke character. Hypothesis: fill dabs + many piles mixing wet-in-wet on the brush smear everything. Don't use fill=true where stroke character matters. Plan: let dry, then hatch over without fill, cov ~0.9.
> - day 29, 07:35: ## Campaign 3 (day 24-29)
>   - Canopy undersides: cDeep (viridian2/ultra1.5/black0.3/red earth0.15/white0.15) flat 8 cov 1.1 over dry: read as heavy navy blots. Then cMid band cov 0.7 load 0.6 softened transition somewhat. Still too uniform navy; needs warmer/greener darks later.
>   - Houses: shadow planes wallShd too grey; shdWarm overlay (white2/ochre1.2/cobalt0.35/red earth0.25/rose0.1) better. Eave ribbons too mechanical; breaking them with short roof dashes gave beads (as studio note 37 warned).
>   - Mountain facets: five hand-drawn facet polys, each hatch flat 8, cov 1.3, edge soft, clip=mtnM:grow(1), over DRY first coat: clear planes; good. Gully ribbons read as claw stripes: bad, repaint.
>   - Foothill band (hatch flat 6) gives the mountain a base.
>   - MISTAKE: plain repaint mask didn't exclude trunks -> trunks painted out from y 320-560. Also worley-cell pile selection with 0.04 off-weights gave confetti, not fields. Hypothesis: worley id selection with scale distortion is too fine; use hand-drawn field polygons instead.
> - day 37, 12:44: ## Campaign 4 (day 37)
>   - Plain repainted as perspective field strips (rows converging to vp 560,300, polys per field, one pile each + pCool far): reads as fields. Then broken hedgerows as random ribbons + converging tree rows (flat 4, len 5-10): readable but dashed/zigzag, a bit mechanical.
>   - Trunks restated (excluded from canopy): now thin straight poles — too stiff.
>   - Foreground over DRY: worley-cell patches (period 105-110, off-weight 0.12), flat 12, len 28-48, cov 1.15, no fill: proper patch structure, strokes keep their ends. Left dark/right light now splits foreground into two flat halves at the road.
>   Scratch: turps 0.4-0.5 piles with hatch over dry green are still near-opaque (ultra+viridian glaze reads solid navy). Hypothesis: with turps alone a coat stays opaque if pigment-rich; transparency needs medium or much white-free low-pigment mix.
>   Next: dry; give trunks curvature/width; foreground structure (bush at right, shadow bands across road), break the left/right split; warm the mint band left of village.
> - day 73, 14:27: ## Campaign 5 (day 45-73)
>   - Trunks rebuilt as tapered ribbons (30->14 wide) with lit/mid/green/dark piles graded across width: rounder. Branch arcs via round w6 gesture, then covered partly with foliage.
>   - Right bush (outline soft, lobe 22) flat 11 cov 1.4: good dark repoussoir.
>   - Pine shadows across road/meadow: first shRoad/shGrass (too pale, read as grey cloth). Scratch: shR2 (white1/cobalt1/ultra0.4/rose0.4/ochre0.2) and shG2 (viridian1/ultra0.6/ochre0.5/white0.4/rose0.1) over dry road color — saturated. Used shR3 (white1.5/cobalt.8/ultra.2/rose.25/ochre.5) + shG2/shG3 in two layers over dry, cov 1.05 then 0.85: reads as shadow now, with gaps of light.
>   - Sky: worley-gated patches (dens by cell id, y-dependent) of skyF/G/H, flat 12 cov 1.0 load 0.8 over DRY sky: strong broken-patch sky, very Cézanne; but heavier than the smooth left sky. A second gated skyK pass at x>470.
>   - Blue contour lines: round 4.5 point 0.5, line pile (ultra1/cobalt.6/white.35/rose.1, medium 0.2), load 0.55, gestures with pressure 0.1-0.6: thin crisp blue lines, broken segments. On scratch over dry: thin, saturated. Works for mountain ridge, trunks, house edges.
> - day 79, 16:15: ## Day 79
>   - FAILED: tree rows as filbert-6 single stroke stamps (one per tree, load 0.5) — read as rows of beads/dots, mechanical. Rag dipped 0.7, w12, wipes along rows p0.7: loaded to 1.0 at once and only smeared a streak; lifted little.
>   - Repair: gated (noise>-0.05) band hatch of each field's own pile, flat 4-8, cov 1.2 wet into the open dots: dissolved most dots into the field color, leaving soft hints of trees. Works.
>   - Whole: plain now a pale yellow/green haze — lost the earlier field structure; low contrast in the middle distance. Village reads. Key open issues: the plain lacks value structure; trunks still rigid straight poles; the sunlit patch at left bottom and right meadow too bright-yellow; road's shadow blue patch is a flat block.
> - day 105, 17:40: ## Day 99-105
>   - Plain: hand-drawn field polys (roughen 2) + gated hedgerow ribbons (noise>-0.15) flat 3-6: clear field structure again; hedgerows a bit regular stripes.
>   - Mountain: worley-gated mixed patch pass (flat 7, cov 0.9, load 0.75, 5 piles weighted by facet) over dry facets -> lively broken patches, but it blurred the light/shadow planes; restated shadow plane B and a ravine with gated mViol pass; blue ridge segments with line2 (more white, paler).
>   - Right meadow: grey-green 'fallow' (white2.5 heavy) read as chalky cloud; vermilion-ochre patch too hot. Overpainted wet-in-wet with gMid/gYel gated strokes cov 0.8-0.9: fused into grey-greens and ochre-greens, acceptable.
>   - Road sun-flecks (road pile ellipses) read as puddles; rimmed with shadow color, partly integrated.
>   Hypothesis: any mixture with white>2 parts over green reads chalky; keep foreground lights warm and saturated.
> - day 145, 20:28: ## Day 115-145
>   - Sky left: worley-gated patch pass (period 60, gate 0.5) as on the right — sky now consistent across.
>   - Blue drawing lines in canopy (line2, round 4) read as wires across sky; wiped at once with rag w8 dipped 0.8, 3 wipes/refolds each: lifted cleanly (thin open line, little paint). Rag works on thin fresh lines, not on thick hatch.
>   - Trunk contours restated with lineT (ultra/red earth/rose/white, medium 0.15) — muted violet; better than electric blue line.
>   - House walls: gated broken pass flat 4 with pink/cool/lit whites cov 0.8 over dry: stone texture. Shadow planes: needed THREE overlays to read dark enough; shdDeep2 (white1/ochre.7/cobalt.8/ultra.2/rose.3) gives a lavender-grey shadow plane with value contrast. Eaves as broken flat-3 dashes of eaveD.
>   - Plain: worley-gated patches (period 45, y*2.2 stretch, gate 0.45), flat 7, 6 piles, scale_at by depth, cov 0.9 load 0.75 over dry: broke the stripes into Cézanne-like mosaic fields. Best recipe for the plain so far.
> - day 165, 21:11: ## Handoff (day 165, end of sitting)
>   State: all paint dry (14-day wait after last touches). Signed bottom left in red-earth/ultramarine (round 2.5).
>   Unresolved passages:
>   - Mountain is too symmetrical and cone-like; its left slope is one long even line. Could add a shoulder/second summit or tilt planes more.
>   - Houses still read a bit like cut-out blocks (clipped poly edges). Passage at their bases (ground color slipping over wall bottoms) would help.
>   - Trunk 1 has a thin blue contour wire at y 250-420 outside the trunk's shadow side; trunks still straight and parallel.
>   - Right meadow middle (x 600-900, y 560-620) is a flat yellow-green; the road's lit upper stretch has a pale hard boundary on its right.
>   - Canopy: fairly uniform pattern of rounded patches; upper-left canopy's lit/dark rhythm repeats.
>   Practical lessons (hypotheses unless noted):
>   - Best recipe for Cézanne patch structure here: worley-cell gated hatch passes (gate on cell id, pile chosen by cell id with off-weight 0.05), flat 7-12, length 14-46, coverage 0.9-1.15, load 0.7-0.8, NO fill, over DRY paint. Observed in sky, plain, mountain, road, foreground.
>   - fill=true + many piles over a wet/tacky layer => smeary haze (observed once, foreground day 12).
>   - Rag lifts thin fresh lines well (dipped 0.6-0.8, several wipes with refolds); did not lift thick fresh hatch (coverage 1.8) noticeably. Knife scrape p0.95 also lifted little from that.
>   - Mixtures with lead white >2 parts in the foreground read chalky/cloud-like over greens; keep foreground lights warm and pigment-rich.
>   - Shadow planes on light walls needed three overlays; one pass of a mid lavender does little because lead white walls are high-key.
>   - Single-stroke 'stamps' for distant trees read as beads; wet-into-wet field-color hatch dissolved them (good repair).
>   - Unclipped hatch overruns: always subtract trunks/houses from masks of adjacent passes (day 29 trunks painted out by a plain pass).
> - day 185, 22:05: ## Day 165-185: closing sitting. Judgements on the unresolved passages
>   - Mountain too cone-like: IMPROVED. Drew a new right shoulder poly above the old right slope (ridge 648,167 -> dip ~784,192 -> knoll 800,186 -> long falling ridge to 1000,231), with a lower edge 18 units into the old mountain. Filled it over DRY sky/mountain with a worley-gated mixed hatch (period 30, flat 8, cov 1.35, load 0.8, edge firm, piles mtLit/mPale/mPink/mOchG/mViol chosen by cell). It covered the sky fully at one pass. Then a gated violet plane under the shoulder (flat 7, cov 1.0) and broken line2 ridge segments (round 4.5, load 0.45). The mountain now reads as a massif with a long shoulder and is asymmetric. It's the best change of the sitting.
>     - A rag (w8, dipped 0.8, 3 wipes with refolds) lifted a fresh blue line cleanly, but it ALSO lifted the violet hatch laid minutes before beneath it, which left a pale streak. Repaired with mViol hatch wet-in-wet. Lesson: the rag lifts every open layer under the line, so put lines only on dry paint if you may want to wipe them.
>   - Houses cut-out: PARTLY IMPROVED, ACCEPTED. Cast shadows to the right of the house bases and dark contact strips (baseSh = shG2 .5 / shadeL .8 / gMid .3, flat 4 hatch, clipped minus housesM) seat the houses on the ground. Gated flat-3 vertical hatch in shdDeep2/hViol/earthW on the shadow sides gave a stone texture. A green fringe hatch ring around the tree masses softens the dark-tree edges. The wall edges are still crisp polys. I accept that: Cézanne's houses are crisp blocks too.
>   - Trunk 1 blue wire: REPAIRED. Covered at y 174-305 with trDk/trMid hatch, flat 4, cov 1.6 over dry, then trMid/trLit on the left half. The trunk is now continuous and round there. The thin blue horizontal 'wire' lines in the canopy (y~193, ~290, ~255) were covered: canopy hatch inside the canopy, sky hatch outside. My first sky pile (skyB/skyH/skyC, horizontal) left pale bars, so I re-hatched with skyE/skyK/skyG at angle -1.1 wet-in-wet, which merged them.
>   - Trunks straight and parallel: ACCEPTED. Their slight lean and taper is enough to frame the view, and rebuilding the trunks risks more than it gives.
>   - Right meadow flat yellow-green: IMPROVED. A worley-gated patch pass over dry paint (period 40, y*2, gate 0.55, flat 8, cov 0.9, load 0.75, gMid/cOlive/shadeL/earthW/gDeepW/pRose by cell) gave it a mosaic of planes. The recipe confirmed again.
>   - Canopy pattern repetition: ACCEPTED as it is.
>   All paint dry at day 185.
> - day 185, 22:05: ## Handoff (day 185, finished)
>   Title: The Village below the Mountain, with Two Pines. All dry, signed lower left.
>   Reflection: I'm happy with it. The mountain shoulder gave the right half the weight it lacked. The picture now reads as a stable, built landscape of warm and cool patches, framed by the pines. What remains: the trunks are a little stiff, the house edges crisp, the canopy's rhythm repetitive. I accept all three as part of the picture's plainness.
>   Practical lessons still in force (hypotheses unless noted):
>   - Patch structure: worley-gated hatch over DRY paint, flat 7-12, length 14-46, cov 0.9-1.35, load 0.7-0.8, no fill, pile chosen by cell id (off-weight 0.05). Confirmed many times.
>   - fill=true + many piles over tacky paint => haze (seen once).
>   - A rag lifts thin fresh lines, and also any OPEN paint beneath them. Thick hatch (cov 1.8) barely lifts.
>   - Foreground lights with lead white >2 parts look chalky over greens.
>   - Pale walls need about three shadow overlays. Cast/contact shadows at the bases seat houses.
>   - Always subtract trunks/houses/canopy from masks of adjacent passes.
> - day 197, 22:08: ## Day 185-197: short return sitting
>   Fresh look: the whole holds; the mountain shoulder, the village and the frame of pines still work. The one passage I'd listed unresolved and never judged was the road's lit upper stretch, a pale wedge with a ruler-straight right edge.
>   - Road right edge: IMPROVED. Over DRY paint, I made a band about 30 units wide along the edge (xr = 612+(y-620)*1.08; for y<615 I used an approximate line). I gated it by worley cells (period 13-15, y*1.3, gate 0.42-0.45). Where the band lay inside the road I painted "bites" of meadow (pOlive/cOlive/gMid/shG2, flat 6-7, len 10-20, cov 1.1, load 0.75). Where it lay outside, half the cells got "pushes" of road colour (roadPk/roadLit2/earthW, cov 1.0). This redraws the contour instead of feathering it. An earlier lose() with gYel had only added an acid lime strip. Result: the road's top now runs into the grass, and the edge is irregular and believable. The outer pink dabs read as stones or dust. There are slightly too many, but I accept them because at full view they don't show.
>   - Thin blue hairline contours on the house verticals: INSPECTED at full detail and ACCEPTED. They are hairlines along the shadow-side edges and read as Cézanne's blue drawing. They're barely visible at full view.
>   - Trunks straight, canopy rhythm, crisp house edges: still accepted, for the reasons I gave at day 185.
>   All dry at day 197.
>   Lesson (one observation): to get rid of a straight mask edge, redraw it by gated bites and pushes across it. Feathering with lose() kept the line and added a strip of colour.
> - day 197, 22:08: ## Handoff (day 197, finished)
>   Title: The Village below the Mountain, with Two Pines. All dry, signed lower left.
>   Reflection: my heart is happy with it. This sitting only made one quiet repair, to the road's edge, and the picture didn't need more. If I came back, the trunks' stiffness is the one thing I'd enjoy taking further. I'd do it only with a full plan for both trunks, not as patching.

>   Plan: redraw both trunks along new smooth centrelines (Catmull-Rom through hand-placed points: nt1, nt2). Trunk 1 now bends: it leans left at the base (x116 at y805), straightens to vertical around y 400-500 (x 164) and turns right into the canopy (x 193 at y 100). Trunk 2 leans gently right (244 -> 304). Different curves, not mirrored. The old trunk strips that would be exposed were covered first, then the new trunks painted.
>   - Covering the old trunks: SCRATCH trial (orange trunk band dry 30 days, then green/sky hatch, flat 7, cov 1.4-2.0, load 0.8). cov 1.4 without fill left orange showing between strokes. fill=true at cov 1.4 covered it completely. Two crossing passes without fill covered it too. On the painting I used fill=true, flat 6, cov 1.4, with the zone's own piles by worley cell, split into height bands (canopy/sky/hills/plain/bank/foreground). It covered completely, but each strip read as a smooth vertical BLOCK (fill makes an even film). Over DRY paint, a gated worley patch pass (period 30, gate 0.62, cov 1.0, load 0.75) over a band 14 units around the strip broke most of it. Two later gated passes, 30 and 34 units wide in the plain/hill band (y 300-562), dissolved the last vertical ghost edges, which I checked in squint. Lesson (one observation): fill hides an underlayer but leaves a block shape. Follow it, once dry, with a wider gated patch pass that crosses the block's edges.
>   - New trunks: SCRATCH trial of three bark recipes on dry green. (a) Graded trLit/trMid/trDk with orange/violet broken overlay: hot orange and black-violet, too strong. (b) and (c) Base hatch flat 5, cov 2.2, fill, graded by normalised across-position u in 4 bands: barkL (white2/ochre1.2/red earth.6/vermilion.1) on the lit left, trLit, trMid, trShd on the right. Once dry, a gated overlay (worley period 13 stretched along the trunk, flat 5, cov 1.0) of pRose/earthW/trGreen/barkV gave a round, warm-cool bark. The barkV overlay dots on the shadow side read too blue-violet and blotchy. Recipe (c) was chosen. On the painting the stroke angle follows the axis (axisAng from a lookup table). Fresh look at the whole and detail crops in normal colour (upper-right sky 500-1000 x 0-250; pine 2 crown; foreground left and right; road in shadow; village).
- Upper-right sky "too busy?": INSPECTED, ACCEPTED. At 1:1 the strokes are light, broken blue/cream/grey-green patches tilted one way. At full view they make an active sky that balances the dark pine canopy at upper left and pushes against the mountain's calm planes. If I calmed it, the right half would go slack.
- Pine 2 crown (repaired last sitting): it holds, with a warm lit top and limbs showing in fragments. The twig streak and the sky hole are still accepted.
- Road in shadow, lower edges (crop 500-880 x 650-800): the edges are already broken by green patches and ochre dashes. No straight ruler line. Accepted.

content.text:
**The Village below the Mountain, with Two Pines** is finished as it stood. I didn't lay any paint this sitting.

I looked at the whole canvas and at full-detail close-ups of the upper-right sky, the smaller pine's crown, both halves of the foreground, the shadowed road and the village.

- **Upper-right sky:** last time I left open whether it was too busy. I've decided to keep it as it is. Its broken, tilted patches give the right side some movement against the heavy pine canopy at upper left and the mountain's calm planes. If I quietened it, that half of the picture would go flat.
- **Small pine's crown:** last sitting's repair still works. Its lit top agrees with the big pine about where the sun is.
- **Shadowed road:** green and ochre patches already break up its edges, so there's no ruled line to fix.
- **Houses:** I still accept their crisp edges as part of the picture's plain, built quality.

My heart is happy with it, and I can't see anything I'd enjoy taking further. More marks now would just be fiddling. The journal has this sitting's judgements and the handoff, with the practical lessons that still apply:
- broken patch strokes laid over dry paint
- breaking up straight edges by working across them
- what a rag can and can't lift
- keeping foreground lights warm rather than chalky
- three shadow layers on pale walls
- always masking out neighbouring objects
